ai_overview.text: asyncio is a built-in Python library used to write concurrent code using the async and await syntax . Python documentation Unlike multiprocessing or traditional threading, asyncio is single-threaded and single-process . It achieves concurrency through cooperative multitasking managed by a single mechanism called an event loop. YouTube · Corey Schafer +2 The Event Loop: The central coordinator (like an orchestra conductor) that manages and distributes the execution of different tasks. It runs one task at a time; when that task hits a blocking operation, it yields control back to the loop, which switches to another pending task. Python documentation +1 Coroutines: Functions declared with async def . Calling an async function does not execute it immediately; instead, it returns a coroutine object that must be explicitly run or awaited. YouTube · Tech With Tim +2 The await Keyword: Used to pause the execution of a coroutine. It tells the event loop: "I am waiting for this external operation to finish. Go ahead and run something else in the meantime." Medium · Rohit Kushwaha +2 Concurrency Model Best Used For How It Works asyncio I/O-bound tasks (e.g., scraping web pages, API requests, database queries) Single thread. Tasks cooperatively hand off control while waiting for external resources. threading I/O-bound tasks with legacy code or blocking libraries. Multiple threads. The operating system forcefully switches between threads (preemptive multitasking). multiprocessing CPU-bound tasks (e.g., heavy math, machine learning, image processing) Spreads work across multiple CPU cores to achieve true parallelism. To execute an asynchronous program, you initiate the event loop using asyncio.run() . Non-blocking pauses are simulated using asyncio.sleep() instead of the standard standard time.sleep() (which would freeze the entire thread). YouTube · NeuralNine +3 python import asyncio async def fetch_data ( id ): print( f " Starting fetch for item {id} ... " ) # Simulate a network request (non-blocking pause) await asyncio.sleep( 2 ) print( f " Finished fetch for item {id} ! " ) return { " data " : id} async def main (): # Modern Python 3.11+ approach using Task Groups to run concurrently async with asyncio.TaskGroup() as tg : task1 = tg.create_task(fetch_data( 1 )) task2 = tg.create_task(fetch_data( 2 )) # Both tasks run concurrently; total wait time is ~2 seconds, not 4. print(task1.result()) print(task2.result()) # Entry point to kick off the event loop asyncio.run(main()) Use code with caution. It's not parallel processing: It does not run multiple lines of code at the exact same physical millisecond. It maximizes idle waiting periods to get more work done. YouTube · Corey Schafer +1 It requires async libraries: To benefit from asyncio , the packages you use must also be asynchronous (e.g., using httpx or aiohttp instead of requests for web calls).
